activity.title: Reaching 100,000 X followers in two years feels a bit like a miracle. Thank you all. Since this isn’t something that happens every day I wanted to share a more personal message. When I started this, my goal was simply to learn and build something useful for myself. With no development experience and no expectation that I could even create the radar tool (let alone that anyone would see it), I tried building it openly as I taught myself to code. Thanks to you, this little personal experiment with no team, funding, marketing, or business plan, just kept growing organically - way beyond anything I could have ever imagined • 2.5 million users • 8 million page views • A comprehensive suite of tools trusted by hundreds of subscribers monthly • A growing community of 120,000+ followers across socials The journey has been unbelievable. Today, DataMB is trusted by top-tier clubs, players, and agents worldwide, featured in major publications, and has formed partnerships at the highest levels of football. Scouts from the club I've supported my entire life are now subscribers. So many surreal things have happened, it’s tough to even keep track. And beyond my passion for football, this platform has also allowed me to give back and create opportunities for others and supporting people in ways I never anticipated when I first started coding. None of this would exist without you. A massive thank you to everyone who has been part of this journey: subscribers, users, and followers; contributors, interns, and partners; and every single person who has shared the platform, offered feedback, or helped me improve along the way. Your trust and support mean everything. I'm not sure I'll ever fully understand how this all happened, but I've been extremely fortunate. And I believe that comes with a responsibility to make the most of it. For two years, I have lived and breathed DataMB, and I will continue to work tirelessly to improve every day and deliver the best possible experience. We've come a long way from the first tentative radar tool, yet the platform is still barely scratching the surface of its potential. This is still just the very beginning, the to-do list is longer than ever as there are still countless improvements needed both in terms of fixes and additions. But the fact that hundreds of you find it valuable enough to subscribe every month is what drives me to keep building. I will never take that for granted. And if this is what year two looks like, I can't wait to see what comes next. But this milestone is the perfect moment to pause and personally say thank you. I am truly grateful, and committed to repaying your trust and making sure DataMB remains organic, transparent and accessible. Your feedback has always guided my direction, and it always will. If you want to get in touch, or have any questions, don't hesitate to reach out! Olivier — DataMB datamb.football ...more ...more

Excellent writeup from Yuhao Chen. This is one of the clearest mental models I've seen for making sense of the omni/audio model landscape. What impresses me most is the maturity of the abstraction. Anyone can list the differences between Qwen3-Omni, Fish S2-Pro, MOSS-TTS, Higgs, Voxtral, Ming-Omni and dots.tts - the papers hand you those. It takes much deeper understanding to strip away the implementation noise and see that speech-in → speech-out almost always reduces to Audio Encoding → Thinker → Talker → Audio Decoding, that the variation concentrates in the Talker, and that Talkers fall into just two families (discrete codec tokens vs continuous acoustic latents) which are already converging in models like Voxtral. The inference framing is what makes it genuinely useful rather than just tidy: whether a Talker is discrete or continuous determines whether you can reuse the LLM serving stack or whether iterative denoising dominates your latency path. That's the distinction that actually shapes optimization work. Yuhao has been learning at a remarkable pace and building real depth fast - this article is strong evidence of that. Worth a read for anyone working on speech inference: https://lnkd.in/gRRD9T_4

Introducing Deepgram Flux TTS, a text-to-speech model built for live conversation. Voice AI is moving from demos to real customer calls, and the bar there is different. Text-to-speech needs to be able to handle the nuances of how we speak. Can it handle interruptions? A changed order? A string of numbers read off fast? Can it respond quickly enough, and sound expressive enough, to feel like a real conversation? Flux TTS was built for exactly that. It tracks context across turns, adapts mid-call, carries natural expressiveness, and responds in as low as 80ms. These are voices you'll want to have a conversation with. Build with Flux TTS for free until September 12th: https://lnkd.in/eJvR2b-j Also, I asked Flux about Flux. Hear what it had to say.

Patrick Collison on how Stripe got its name: "We just couldn't come up with a good name... We were literally reduced to picking random words late at night." "One of the folks at Stripe had the bright idea of, 'Why don't we just assemble a big list of words and email all of the owners of the dot com domains?'" "And then we also continued our own creative process. We came up with memorable names like PayDemon... We thought it was super clever because we could have this awesome mascot." "The owner of stripe.com generously responded to us and had an offer that was at least within our plausible budgetary range." "But we couldn't decide between PayDemon and Stripe. I swear I'm not making this up... If we could not settle on a name by December 20th, 2010, we would just default to Stripe. And we couldn't think of a more compelling name, and so Stripe it became." Patrick Collison w/ John Lilly at Stanford University (2015)

Another one down: Levit and Mandrescu's conjecture that every very well-covered graph has a unimodal independence polynomial is false. For the whiskering of E₅₈₈ ∨ (39K₁₁ ⊔ 85K₁₂), a graph on 4,074 vertices with independence polynomial (1 + x)¹⁴⁴⁹(1 + 2x)⁵⁸⁸ + (1 + x)¹⁹¹³(1 + 12x)³⁹(1 + 13x)⁸⁵ − (1 + x)²⁰³⁷, there exists a strict local valley a₁₀₉₄ > a₁₀₉₅ < a₁₀₉₆. Thanks to our friends GPT 5.6 Sol and Claude Fable 5, as well as our human reviewers, for their hard work. We are proud to be participating in the development of proof automation for mathematical discovery. (Fun fact: once the question was posed, the solution took only a few hours, namely until 9pm ET last Wednesday.)
